name: Earliest Greek Papyri
description: The oldest surviving New Testament manuscripts, predating the great codices; their text typically aligns with the Alexandrian tradition later preserved in Vaticanus and Sinaiticus, and has shaped every modern critical edition.

name: Codex Vaticanus
primarySource: Parchment codex, Vatican Library (MS Vat.gr.1209); Alexandrian text type throughout
description: One of the oldest and most complete Greek Bibles; a primary witness to the Alexandrian text type and a cornerstone of the Westcott-Hort critical text and all subsequent eclectic editions.

name: Codex Sinaiticus
primarySource: Parchment codex discovered at St. Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, 1844; Alexandrian text with Western influence
description: The most complete ancient Greek NT manuscript, discovered by Tischendorf in 1844; jointly foundational with Vaticanus for the Westcott-Hort critical text and all modern eclectic editions.

name: Vulgate (Jerome)
primarySource: Latin translation by Jerome, commissioned by Pope Damasus I 382 CE; NT revised against Greek originals; OT from Hebrew
description: The standard Latin Bible of the Western Church for over a millennium, translated by Jerome from the Greek (NT) and Hebrew (OT); the direct ancestor of the Clementine Vulgate, the Stuttgart critical edition, and all medieval Western translations.

name: Peshitta
primarySource: Standard Syriac Bible of the Eastern churches; NT text associated with Antiochene Syriac Christianity
description: The ancient Syriac translation that became the authoritative Bible of Syriac Christianity; the NT Peshitta reflects a text close to the Byzantine tradition and was first critically edited by Gwilliam in 1905.

name: Byzantine Text Form
primarySource: Majority text type preserved in thousands of Greek manuscripts copied in the Byzantine empire through the medieval period
description: The dominant Greek text tradition of the medieval church, represented by the overwhelming majority of surviving Greek manuscripts; the basis for Erasmus's printed Greek NT, the Textus Receptus, and the modern Byzantine Priority critical text.

name: Wycliffe Bible
primarySource: John Wycliffe and associates; translated from the Latin Vulgate into Middle English; handwritten copies only
description: The first complete English Bible, translated from the Latin Vulgate by John Wycliffe's circle at Oxford; handwritten (printing was not yet invented in England), it established English as a viable language for scripture over fierce church opposition.

name: Erasmus Greek New Testament
primarySource: Desiderius Erasmus; compiled from 5–6 Byzantine manuscripts in Basel; five editions 1516–1535; parallel Greek and Latin columns
description: The first printed Greek NT, produced by Erasmus using a small set of Byzantine manuscripts; hastily compiled but enormously influential, it established the printed Greek text for the Reformation and was the direct source for Tyndale's English NT.

name: Tyndale New Testament
primarySource: William Tyndale; translated directly from Erasmus's Greek NT with reference to Luther's German Bible and the Vulgate; printed in Worms
description: The first printed English NT translated directly from Greek; Tyndale's idiomatic and accurate translation shaped English biblical vocabulary so profoundly that scholars estimate up to 75–80% of KJV language traces back to Tyndale.

name: Stephanus Greek New Testament
primarySource: Robert Estienne (Stephanus); compared Erasmus's text with 15 manuscripts including Codex Bezae and a Vaticanus collation; 1550 'Royal Edition'
description: Robert Estienne's 1550 Royal Edition introduced verse divisions still in universal use today; his 1551 edition first divided the NT into individual verses. Estienne's text became the primary Greek base for the KJV translators (via Beza 1598).

name: Geneva Bible
primarySource: Marian exiles in Geneva, led by William Whittingham; revised Tyndale using Beza's Latin NT and Stephanus's Greek text; first English Bible with verse numbers
description: The most widely read English Bible before the KJV, used by the Pilgrims and Shakespeare; its Calvinist annotations and typographical innovations (verse numbers, roman type, italics for supplied words) made it the preferred Protestant Bible and a major reference for the KJV translators.

name: Beza Greek New Testament
primarySource: Theodore Beza; ten editions 1565–1611; primary Greek text relied upon by the KJV translators (especially the 1598 edition)
description: The most immediate predecessor to the KJV, Beza's Greek NT was essentially a revised Stephanus. The KJV committee relied primarily on his 1598 edition. Together with Stephanus and Erasmus, Beza's work constitutes the Textus Receptus stream before Elzevir gave it that name in 1633.

name: Bishops' Bible
primarySource: Produced by a committee of Church of England bishops under Archbishop Matthew Parker; a revision of the Great Bible (1539) and Tyndale's English tradition; the KJV translators were instructed to follow it as their base text
description: The official Church of England Bible before the KJV, and the formal English base the KJV translators were required to start from. The KJV was primarily a revision of the Bishops' Bible against Beza's Greek text; it represents the culmination of the Tyndale–Coverdale–Great Bible English revision chain.

name: Douay-Rheims Bible
primarySource: English College at Douai and Rheims; NT published Rheims 1582, OT published Douai 1609–1610; translated from the Latin Vulgate
description: The first complete Catholic English Bible, translated from the Latin Vulgate rather than the original Greek and Hebrew. Note: the NT (1582) predates the Clementine Vulgate (1592) and was based on available pre-Clementine manuscripts; the OT (1609–1610) postdates and reflects the Clementine tradition.

name: Clementine Vulgate
primarySource: Authorized revision issued under Pope Clement VIII; official Catholic scriptural text until the Stuttgart critical edition in the 20th century
description: The officially authorized edition of the Latin Vulgate issued by Pope Clement VIII after the flawed Sixtine edition (1590) was recalled; it served as the definitive Catholic scriptural text for nearly four centuries.

name: King James Version
primarySource: 47 scholars in six companies; English base: Bishops' Bible, heavily revised against Tyndale and Geneva; Greek base: Beza 1598 and Stephanus 1550; standard text established 1769
description: The most influential English translation in history; the KJV synthesized two streams — the Bishops' Bible English revision tradition and Beza's printed Greek text — into a literary standard that shaped English prose for four centuries. Note: the Elzevir Textus Receptus (1633) postdates the KJV; the KJV's Greek base was Beza (1598) and Stephanus (1550).

name: Textus Receptus (Elzevir)
primarySource: Bonaventure and Abraham Elzevir, Leiden; essentially a reprint of Beza (1565/1589) and Stephanus; preface coined 'textum ergo habes, nunc ab omnibus receptum'
description: The Elzevir brothers' 1633 edition coined the phrase 'Textus Receptus' (received text); it gave a formal name to the Byzantine-based printed Greek text that Protestant translations had used for a century, and became the explicit textual standard for three more centuries of translation, including the NKJV (1982).

name: Challoner Revision
primarySource: Bishop Richard Challoner; extensively revised the Douay-Rheims Bible in multiple editions (1749–1763); modernized archaic language and corrected Latinisms; the Challoner revision became the standard Catholic English Bible in England and America until the 20th century
description: The Challoner revision so extensively reworked the Douay-Rheims that it is sometimes treated as a separate translation. By modernizing vocabulary and syntax while retaining the Vulgate-based approach, Challoner made the Catholic English Bible practically accessible for the first time, and it remained in standard use until Vatican II inspired new translations.

name: Westcott-Hort Greek New Testament
primarySource: B.F. Westcott and F.J.A. Hort; 28 years of work; privileged Vaticanus and Sinaiticus as the most reliable witnesses to the original text
description: The critical Greek text that overturned three centuries of Textus Receptus dominance; Westcott and Hort's systematic eclectic method — privileging the Alexandrian text — became the foundation of all modern critical editions and most contemporary English translations.

name: Revised Version
primarySource: British revision committee of 65 scholars; NT 1881, OT 1885; Greek base was the Westcott-Hort critical text, consulted in committee by Westcott and Hort themselves; a formal revision of the KJV
description: The first major English revision of the KJV, produced by a large British committee using the new Westcott-Hort Greek text. Its American counterpart became the ASV (1901). The RV–ASV line is the direct ancestor of the RSV (1952), NASB (1971), NRSV (1989), and ESV (2001) revision chains.

name: Nestle-Aland Novum Testamentum Graece
primarySource: Eberhard Nestle (1898) through Barbara Aland et al. (NA28, 2012); eclectic critical text incorporating all major manuscript discoveries
description: The standard scholarly Greek NT, now in its 28th edition; the primary source text for most modern translations. Nestle's original method combined Westcott-Hort, Tischendorf, and Weiss; subsequent editions incorporated papyri discoveries. The date 1898 represents the start of the tradition; NA28 was published 2012.

name: American Standard Version
primarySource: American revision of the British Revised Version (1881/1885); the RV/ASV committee used the Westcott-Hort text as their Greek base
description: The American counterpart to the British Revised Version; its aim was a more literal revision of the KJV using the new critical Greek text. The ASV became the direct parent of the RSV (1952), NASB (1971), and ESV (2001) revision chains, making it a key bridge between the KJV tradition and modern critical-text translations.

name: BFBS Critical Peshitta
primarySource: Philip E. Pusey and G.H. Gwilliam; collated over 40 manuscripts; published by the British and Foreign Bible Society 1901–1905
description: The first critical edition of the Peshitta NT, establishing a scholarly text by collating the best available manuscripts; it remains the standard academic Peshitta text and the foundation of all subsequent Peshitta scholarship and translation.

name: Revised Standard Version
primarySource: National Council of Churches; formal revision of the American Standard Version (1901), itself a KJV revision; NT used the eclectic critical Greek text
description: A revision of the American Standard Version (1901) — itself a KJV descendant — the RSV aimed for literary quality while incorporating critical textual scholarship. Its 1952 NT became the dominant scholarly English Bible, directly spawning the NRSV (1989) and ESV (2001).

name: Good News Bible (Today's English Version)
primarySource: American Bible Society; Robert Bratcher principal translator of the NT (1966); dynamic equivalence approach aimed at readers without a church background; OT completed 1976
description: The first widely distributed dynamic equivalence English translation, produced by the American Bible Society for readers unfamiliar with religious vocabulary. Its NT (1966) pioneered the 'common language' approach that influenced the CEV, NLT, and The Message. Translated from the NA/UBS critical Greek text throughout.

name: Jerusalem Bible
primarySource: English Dominican scholars under Alexander Jones; translated from the French Bible de Jérusalem (1956) with direct reference to Hebrew and Greek originals; first Catholic English Bible from originals rather than the Vulgate
description: A landmark Catholic translation produced by English Dominicans working from the French Jerusalem Bible (1956) and the original Hebrew and Greek texts. The first major Catholic English Bible to translate directly from the originals rather than the Vulgate. Noted for its literary quality; J.R.R. Tolkien contributed to the translation of Jonah.

name: New American Standard Bible
primarySource: Lockman Foundation; 58 scholars; NT published 1963, complete Bible 1971; rigidly literal revision of the ASV using the NA critical text; updated NASB95 published 1995
description: A conservative evangelical revision of the ASV pursuing word-for-word accuracy; the most literally exact of the major modern translations. The NASB95 update clarified archaic pronouns while retaining the ASV's formal equivalence philosophy. It is the direct parent of the Legacy Standard Bible (LSB 2021).

name: Biblia Sacra Vulgata (Stuttgart)
primarySource: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft; scholarly eclectic edition reconstructing Jerome's original Vulgate from manuscript evidence
description: The standard modern critical edition of the Latin Vulgate, replacing the Clementine as the academic reference text; its goal is to reconstruct Jerome's original text rather than the authorized Clementine edition, and it is consulted by contemporary translation committees as a secondary Latin reference.

name: New International Version
primarySource: Committee on Bible Translation (CBT); fresh translation (not a revision) by 100+ evangelical scholars from multiple denominations; eclectic Greek text; thoroughly revised 2011
description: A completely fresh translation from the original languages, not a revision of any prior English Bible; its dynamic equivalence approach aimed at natural contemporary English. The best-selling modern English Bible, thoroughly revised in 2011, it used the Nestle-Aland eclectic text tradition throughout.

name: New King James Version
primarySource: Thomas Nelson; 130 scholars; modernizes KJV English while retaining the Textus Receptus (Byzantine majority) Greek base
description: A modernization of the KJV that retains the Textus Receptus Greek base; notable for its transparency — footnotes compare TR readings to the Critical Text (NA) and Majority Text, making textual differences visible to readers.

name: New Revised Standard Version
primarySource: National Council of Churches; revision of RSV incorporating gender-inclusive language for human referents and updated textual scholarship
description: A revision of the RSV that introduced gender-inclusive language for human beings while retaining the RSV's literary register; adopted as the standard ecumenical and academic English Bible by Catholic, Protestant, and Orthodox scholars for study and liturgy.

name: New Living Translation
primarySource: Tyndale House Publishers; 90 scholars; a complete re-translation of the Living Bible (Ken Taylor, 1971) from the original languages using a thought-for-thought approach; NT from NA/UBS critical text
description: A dynamic equivalence translation produced by retranslating the paraphrase Living Bible directly from the Hebrew and Greek. By grounding Taylor's popular idiomatic rendering in the original texts, the NLT achieved both accessibility and scholarly credibility. Revised substantially in 2004 and 2015.

name: World English Bible
primarySource: Michael Paul Johnson; public domain revision of the ASV (1901) with NT updated to the Byzantine Majority Text (Robinson-Pierpont); completed 2000, ongoing updates
description: A public-domain update of the ASV (1901) designed to remove copyright restrictions while updating archaic language. The NT was retranslated against the Byzantine Majority Text rather than the NA critical text, making the WEB a readable modern representative of the Byzantine priority tradition. One of the few royalty-free complete English Bibles.

name: English Standard Version
primarySource: Crossway; conservative revision of the RSV (1971 text) restoring traditional gender language; Greek base: NA27
description: A conservative evangelical revision of the RSV that reversed gender-inclusive language changes; its essentially literal translation philosophy and literary quality made it the preferred study Bible for Reformed and conservative evangelical communities; revised to a 'permanent' text in 2016.

name: The Message
primarySource: Eugene H. Peterson; translated from Greek and Hebrew by a single scholar; NT published 1993, complete Bible 2002; intended as a reading Bible in the idiom of contemporary American English
description: A single-scholar paraphrase that renders Scripture in contemporary American street idiom rather than traditional Bible English. Peterson worked from the Greek and Hebrew texts throughout; while frequently criticized by those who prefer formal equivalence, The Message has introduced millions of non-readers to the Bible as literature.

name: NET Bible (New English Translation)
primarySource: Biblical Studies Press; team of 25+ evangelical scholars; Greek base NA27/NA28; the NET Bible contains over 60,000 translators' notes — more than any other Bible in history — explaining every significant textual and translation decision
description: A fresh translation distinguished by its extraordinary scholarly apparatus: over 60,000 translators' notes that expose every significant textual variant, translation choice, and exegetical decision. The first Bible drafted entirely on the internet, released free online. Its transparency makes it uniquely valuable for comparative textual study.

name: Robinson-Pierpont Byzantine Priority
primarySource: Maurice A. Robinson and William G. Pierpont; Byzantine priority methodology arguing the majority text best preserves the original; 2005 and 2018 editions
description: A critical edition constructed on the principle that the Byzantine majority text best preserves the original NT; the leading academic case for Byzantine priority, and the Greek text base for some Orthodox translations and NKJV-tradition scholarship.

name: New American Bible Revised Edition
primarySource: Catholic Biblical Association of America; OT revised 2011, NT 1986; translated from the original Hebrew and Greek with reference to the Vulgate; approved for Catholic liturgical use in the United States
description: The standard Catholic Bible in American liturgical use, translated directly from the Hebrew and Greek rather than the Vulgate. The Revised Edition (2011) updated the OT translation begun in the original NAB (1970). Its NT (revised 1986) is the translation used in the Lectionary for Mass in the United States.

name: Christian Standard Bible
primarySource: Holman Bible Publishers; 100 scholars; Greek base NA28/UBS5; revision of the Holman Christian Standard Bible (HCSB 2004) with improved readability; 'Optimal Equivalence' translation philosophy
description: A complete revision of the HCSB (2004), pursuing what its translators call 'Optimal Equivalence' — formal where possible, dynamic where necessary for natural English. Adopted by the Southern Baptist Convention as its preferred Bible, the CSB has gained wide evangelical acceptance as a readable yet accurate alternative to the ESV and NIV.

name: Legacy Standard Bible
primarySource: Three16 Publishing; revision of the NASB95; produced under the oversight of John MacArthur and The Master's Seminary; maximally literal word-for-word rendering; restores 'LORD' as 'Yahweh' throughout
description: A maximally literal revision of the NASB95, designed for serious word-for-word study. Its most distinctive feature is rendering the divine name as 'Yahweh' throughout the OT rather than 'LORD', restoring the proper name where the MT has the Tetragrammaton. Represents the terminus of the ASV → NASB literal-translation chain.
